newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock markets to pause after HK handover.
newsitem.headline: China stock markets to pause after HK handover.

text.p: China's stock markets will likely pause for breath in July following the Hong Kong handover and consolidate around current levels while awaiting fresh leads, brokers said on Friday.
"There won't be much activity for a little while," said an analyst at an Asian securities firm in Shanghai.
"If there's a new listing, things might get lively, but investors are waiting for a firm long-term trend," he said.
Market uncertainty stems from rumours that the govenment could be planning further steps to root speculators out of the market, despite the end of euphoria over the Hong Kong handover.

Foreign currency B shares and domestic currency A shares surged earlier this year on the belief that Beijing would support the booming stock markets ahead of July 1, when the British colony of Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule.
Market regulators in May were forced to step up measures against share speculation to stem the buying frenzy.

Brokers said a series of other events could also provide future direction -- the reporting of interim results beginning in July, a major Chinese Communist Party meeting expected in October and a possible cut in interest rates before the end of 1997.

Interim results for the first half of 1997 for both A and B share companies are generally expected to improve from 1996, but buying will be selective in July and August, the month the bulk of firms report, they said.
"In July, people will focus buying on stocks likely to report good earnings," said a stock analyst at the Hainan Province Trust and Investment Co in Shenzhen.
Companies are expected to fare better during the coming results season as the positive benefit from two interest rate cuts last year is more fully felt, analysts said.

But a question mark hangs over the fate of a number of A share firms that listed earlier this year, which investors snapped up and may unload if results give negative clues about their quality, they said.
Overall, investors are expecting the market to be stable ahead of the key Communist party meeting this fall, the first such gathering since the death of Deng Xiaoping, brokers said.
The meeting will seal the legacy of the main leader and could provide important clues on the future development of the economy and the fledging stock markets, they said.
"If they set a clearer policy for economic development, then the market will take it as a good sign," said an analyst from Shenyin & Wanguo Securities Co Ltd in Shanghai.
The major engine for a future rally in China's two stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen would be a possible interest rate cut, but analysts are divided over the timing of any credit loosening.

Current low inflation shows the time is ripe for a cut, which would boost the markets, but the government is trapped between wanting to help state firms and wanting to discourage money from pouring back into shares, they said.
